name: wcp
workload: Recursive copy of 20 x 512MiB files, 7,000 x 1MiB files and 200,000 x 1KiB files on a Samsung NVMe SSD, using io_uring batched reads and writes.
claimed_speedup: 20x512MiB: wcp 3.97s (2579.59 MiB/s) vs cp -r 8.44s (1213.38 MiB/s) vs rsync 17.26s (593.33 MiB/s); 7,000x1MiB: 2.64s vs cp 8.29s vs rsync 13.22s; 200,000x1KiB: 3.92s vs rsync 8.09s vs cp 9.23s; 'Up to 70% faster than cp'
hardware: 64GB RAM, Samsung NVMe SSD (model not given), kernel 5.8 tested
tradeoffs: Linux only, kernel 5.6+; uses a lot of CPU and as much RAM as it can; implementation is 100% non-portable; a command-line tool rather than a library; author says it is not robust enough for daily use.
caveats: First-party numbers from one machine, no benchmark script, cache state and CPU model not stated. Last commit 2021.
found_via: WebSearch: github C file copy tool io_uring faster than cp rsync benchmark parallel copy

name: uring-sync
baseline: GNU coreutils cp -r (local copy) and rsync over SSH (network)
workload: Local copy of 100K small files on NVMe with cold cache using batched io_uring (queue depth 64) plus splice/copy_file_range; network transfer with kernel TLS.
claimed_speedup: Local cold-cache: 100K x 100KB files 5.4s vs cp -r 22.7s (4.2x); 100K x 4KB files 5.14s vs 7.67s (1.5x). Network: 100K files 9.7GB 165s vs rsync 390s (58% faster); 589MB 16.4s vs 24.8s (34% faster); 60MB roughly equal.
hardware: NVMe local copy (CPU model not stated); laptop to GCP VM over public internet for network runs
tradeoffs: Linux only (kernel 5.7+ recommended, kTLS for encryption); needs liburing, libfmt, libssl; a tool not a library; best for many-small-file datasets (ML data).
caveats: Own benchmark script (tests/perf/bench.sh) exists but CPU model and kernel version are not recorded, so tier C. Network numbers depend on a single internet path. Small gains or ties on the smallest datasets. Local-copy numbers appear in README and docs/BENCHMARKS.md.
found_via: WebSearch: github C file copy tool io_uring faster than cp rsync benchmark parallel copy; dev.to/Show HN 'File copier 4x faster than cp using io_uring'

name: FluxIO
baseline: Boost.Asio C++20 file operations; Go os.O_DIRECT with goroutines; POSIX pread/pwrite O_DIRECT fallback
workload: 4KB O_DIRECT sequential and random reads and writes at queue depths 1-128 on a consumer NVMe SSD, using io_uring with SQPOLL and lock-free ring buffers.
claimed_speedup: Sequential write at QD128: 715,827.6 IOPS (2,796.2 MiB/s) vs Go O_DIRECT 239,383.5 IOPS (about 2.99x) vs Boost.Asio 86,783.1 IOPS (about 8.25x); 'over 504,000 IOPS', 'sub-10us latency'
hardware: 'physical NVMe SSD', Core 2 CPU affinity pinning; SSD and CPU models not stated
tradeoffs: Linux io_uring with automatic POSIX O_DIRECT fallback; direct I/O only (4KB aligned); storage engine API, early project (9 commits).
caveats: Baselines are Go and Boost.Asio, not raw pread or fio/liburing, so the win over the named POSIX/io_uring baselines is unproven; no compiler flags or SSD model; very new project. QD128 sequential write is a best case.

name: wudream813/fastio
baseline: std::cin / std::cout (also scanf/printf, fread, getchar_unlocked as rows in the same table)
workload: Reading and writing 100 MiB of about 9.98 million random signed 9-digit integers; the fast read path memory-maps stdin and parses with a 2-byte lookup table.
claimed_speedup: Read 100 MiB: std::cin 565 ms vs mmap+2-byte table 66.5 ms (8.5x) vs fread-buffered 143 ms (3.9x); write: cout 473 ms vs fwrite+4-digit table 148 ms (3.2x). The README header says 69 ms (7.4x) read and 132 ms (3.25x) write for the same library.
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.60 GHz, 2 cores (exact model not stated)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 for competitive programming; mmap path falls back to streaming for pipes and terminals; many compile-time unsafe-speed knobs (e.g. FASTIO_NO_EOF_CHECK).
caveats: Integer-parsing workload, so much of the gain is parsing and formatting rather than file I/O; baseline is cin/cout with default sync (cin with sync off is about equal at 578 ms in its own table); headline numbers differ between README sections; CPU model vague. Repro command: make benchvar.
found_via: WebSearch: github fast file reader C++ faster than ifstream fread mmap benchmark

name: rawscan
workload: Line-by-line scan of an 11.3GB file with 55.6 million lines (82-2525 bytes each) for the pattern '6fffbf42', file already in page cache; measures user CPU time.
claimed_speedup: User CPU: grep 4.38s, fgets 2.61s, getline 2.36s, rawscan 1.60s; 'shaves about 30% to 40% off the user CPU times' compared to fgets and getline
hardware: Ryzen 1700 with ample RAM; 10 runs averaged under nice -n-10
tradeoffs: Near-zero-copy record reader (rs_open, rs_getline, rs_close) using rawmemchr and a read-only sentinel page; GCC and Linux dependent per the README; fixed-size buffers; single-byte delimiter only.
caveats: Measures user CPU time on a cached file, not wall-clock disk throughput; compiler flags not stated on the pages opened; benchmark script is source/tests/compare_various_apis.sh in the repo.

name: file_io_benchmark (m-schuetz)
workload: Randomized-order reads of 1000 chunks of 1MB (1GB total) from an NVMe SSD, comparing fread, memory mapping and unbuffered (FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING) multi-threaded reads on Windows.
claimed_speedup: Multi-threaded: unbuffered 11.3-11.4 GB/s vs memory mapping 6.8-7.3 GB/s vs fread 4.2-5.0 GB/s (disk theoretical max 14.8 GB/s)
tradeoffs: A benchmark of read strategies (harvested winner: unbuffered, multi-threaded, aligned reads), not a reusable library; Windows API specific.
caveats: No license; 2 commits; compiler flags missing; language and last commit date not confirmed from the page opened.

name: SPDK
baseline: Linux kernel io_uring and libaio block I/O (also POSIX I/O)
workload: NVMe 4KB random reads with fio and SPDK perf across queue depths, comparing IOPS per core of the userspace polled-mode NVMe driver against kernel io_uring and libaio.
claimed_speedup: From search snippets of the CHEOPS'23 / SYSTOR'22 papers (snippet only, paper pages blocked): SPDK 305 KIOPS on one core vs 171 KIOPS for the best io_uring configuration; SPDK saturates hardware with 5 cores where io_uring needs 13; '5.5x more IOPS/core than io_uring'; io_uring with kernel polling within 10% of SPDK but at twice the cores.
tradeoffs: Kernel bypass: needs hugepages, dedicated polling cores and a device unbound from the kernel driver; no filesystem or page cache; not a drop-in for POSIX read/write.
caveats: Numbers come only from search snippets of independent papers (atlarge-research.com and ACM pages blocked); the artifact repo https://github.com/atlarge-research/Performance-Characterization-Storage-Stacks (MIT) was opened but its README has no numbers, hardware or flags. The spdk/spdk README makes no numeric claim. Hardware and flags unverified, so verifier should re-open the papers.
